key_terms.meaning: 8-bit register in the 8085 that holds one ALU operand before the operation and the result after it
Five flip-flops S, Z, AC, P, CY that record what happened in the last ALU operation
Carry from bit 3 into bit 4 of the result; used only by the DAA instruction for BCD arithmetic
Set to 1 when the result of an 8-bit operation crosses out of bit 7, or when a borrow occurs
The 8085 pins AD0–AD7 carry the low address byte first, then the data byte, in different T-states of the same machine cycle
Block that generates RD, WR, ALE, IO/M and the other control signals from the decoded instruction and the clock
Block that receives TRAP, RST 7.5, 6.5, 5.5, INTR and drives INTA, and also handles the software interrupts
One period of the processor clock; the smallest timing unit shown in a timing diagram
The group of T-states needed to finish one bus operation such as an opcode fetch, memory read or memory write
Machine cycle of 4 T-states (6 for some instructions) in which the CPU reads the instruction byte from memory
Machine cycle of 3 T-states in which the CPU places an address and reads one data byte from memory
8086 unit that computes physical addresses, fetches instructions into the queue and runs all bus cycles
8086 unit containing the ALU and general registers; it decodes and executes instructions taken from the queue
6-byte FIFO inside the 8086 BIU that holds prefetched instruction bytes waiting for the EU
Input pin that selects minimum mode when tied high (to +5 V) and maximum mode when tied low (to ground)
Chip used in maximum mode; it takes the 8086 status lines S0, S1, S2 and produces the memory and I/O control signals
Chip that divides a crystal or external frequency by 3 to give the 8086 CLK, and also synchronises RESET and READY
Active-low input of a memory chip; the chip drives the data bus only when CS is low and its own read or write input is active
The lowest address of the block assigned to a memory chip; the high address lines must equal this value for the chip to be selected
8086 source index and destination index registers used by string instructions to address the source and destination bytes
Instruction prefix that repeats a string instruction and decrements CX each time until CX becomes zero

takeaways: The 8085 keeps every internal transfer on one 8-bit bus, so registers, ALU and flags are all wired through that single path.
AD0–AD7 carry the low address byte and then data on the same eight pins, which is why an external latch is always needed.
Each 8085 machine cycle has a fixed T-state count: opcode fetch 4 T, memory read 3 T, memory write 3 T, I/O read 3 T, I/O write 3 T.
A timing diagram is read left to right, one T-state at a time; every line shows whether it is a valid address, valid data or a control pulse.
The 8086 splits into a BIU and an EU so that fetching the next instruction overlaps with executing the current one.
Physical address in the 8086 is segment × 16 + offset, which is how 20 address bits come out of 16-bit registers.
Pin 33 (MN/MX) alone decides whether the 8086 generates its own bus control signals or hands status to the 8288.
In both processors a memory chip works only when its chip-select input is active, so address decoding defines the whole memory map.
String instructions with the REP prefix move or compare whole blocks using only SI, DI, CX and the direction flag.
bank_note: Long answers here almost always want a labelled diagram first — 8085 block diagram, 8086 block diagram, a timing diagram, or a memory and I/O interface — followed by a point-by-point working explanation, so practise drawing these quickly and cleanly.

bank.q: Draw the functional block diagram of the 8085 and explain the job of each block, stating clearly why a single 8-bit internal data bus is used.
outline: Block diagram: ALU, accumulator, temporary register, flag register, general registers B C D E H L, stack pointer, program counter
Instruction register and decoder, timing and control, interrupt control, serial I/O control
Address buffer and address/data buffer; AD0–AD7 multiplexed, A8–A15 and ALE
Explanation of the shared 8-bit internal bus and why it reduces pin count and chip cost
Clock inputs X1 X2, RESET IN, READY, HOLD and HLDA mentioned

bank.q: Explain the flag register of the 8085. Give the meaning and use of S, Z, AC, P and CY with one example each.
outline: Five flags and their bit positions in the flag register
S set when bit 7 of result is 1, Z set when result is 00H, P set for even parity
AC is carry out of bit 3, used by DAA for BCD addition
CY set on carry out of bit 7 or on borrow in subtraction
Conditional jump and call instructions that test these flags

bank.q: Draw the timing diagram for the opcode fetch and memory read machine cycles of the 8085 and explain the role of each T-state.
outline: T1: address out on A8–A15 and AD0–AD7, ALE pulse to latch the low byte
T2: RD goes low, AD0–AD7 float and become inputs, status lines IO/M and S0 S1 valid
T3: data sampled from the data bus and transferred to the instruction register or a register
T4: RD returns high, opcode decoded; extra T-states for slow memory through READY
Mark the 4 T-state opcode fetch and the 3 T-state memory read clearly on the diagram

bank.q: Explain the register organisation of the 8086 and give the function of each register group.
outline: General registers AX, BX, CX, DX and their byte halves AH AL etc.
Pointer and index registers SP, BP, SI, DI
Segment registers CS, DS, SS, ES and the meaning of 64 KB segments
IP and the flag register, including the control flags such as IF, DF, TF
Physical address generation: segment × 16 + offset, with one worked example

bank.q: Distinguish minimum mode and maximum mode of the 8086 with the help of the MN/MX pin and the 8288 bus controller.
outline: MN/MX is pin 33; high gives minimum mode, low gives maximum mode
Minimum mode: 8086 itself drives IO/M, WR, RD, ALE, DEN, DT/R and the HOLD/HLDA handshake
Maximum mode: 8086 sends status S0 S1 S2; the 8288 decodes them into MRDC, MWTC, IORC, IOWC and the data-bus enable
Why maximum mode is needed for a coprocessor such as the 8087 and for multiprocessor systems
Lock, queue status and the role of each chip in the two configurations

bank.q: Interface one 4 KB EPROM and one 4 KB RAM to an 8085 system. Show the address decoding, the chip-select logic and the memory map.
outline: Divide the 64 KB space; ROM at 0000H–0FFFH and RAM at 2000H–2FFFH, for example
Twelve address lines to each chip, four high lines to the decoder
Use a 74LS138 or a NAND gate to generate two chip selects
Circuit: 8085 latch, address bus A0–A11, data bus, MEMR and MEMW connected to OE and WE
Memory map table and note on the unused gaps in the map

bank.q: A 6 MHz crystal drives an 8085. Find the T-state time and the time taken by an instruction that needs 7 machine cycles of 3 T-states each.
outline: 8085 clock is the crystal divided by 2, so clock frequency is 3 MHz
T = 1 / 3 MHz = 0.333 µs, that is 333 ns
One machine cycle of 3 T = 1 µs
7 machine cycles = 7 µs
State clearly that all arithmetic carries the unit µs or ns

bank.q: Write an 8086 assembly program using string instructions to copy a block of 20 bytes from an array starting at 3000H to an array starting at 4000H. Explain each instruction.
outline: Set DS and ES to the right segments; use MOV, not LEA, with segment registers
Initialise SI = 3000H, DI = 4000H, CX = 20
CLD to keep the direction flag clear so addresses increase
REP MOVSB to copy; explain that each pass does one byte transfer and decrements CX
Note that REP stops when CX becomes zero and state the final flags

bank.q: Draw the 8086 minimum mode configuration using the 8284 clock generator, three 8282 latches and two 8286 transceivers, and explain the function of each chip.
outline: 8284 divides the crystal by 3 to give CLK and synchronises RESET and READY
Latches hold A0–A19 from the multiplexed AD0–AD15 and A16/S3–A19/S6 lines at the ALE pulse
8286 transceivers buffer the data bus, direction set by DT/R and enabled by DEN
Control signals RD, WR, M/IO generated directly by the processor in minimum mode
Fully labelled diagram with pin names

bank.q: An 8 KB memory chip is connected so that it responds to addresses 8000H to 9FFFH. Identify the base address, the number of address lines needed and the chip-select condition.
outline: 8 KB = 8192 bytes = 2^13, so 13 address lines A0–A12 go to the chip
Base address 8000H in binary
A15 to A13 must be 100 for the chip to be selected
Chip select = A15 · A14′ · A13 with an active-low output
Range check: 8000H + 1FFFH = 9FFFH, matching the given range

bank.q: Compare the 8085 and the 8086 with respect to data bus, address bus, register width, instruction pipelining, memory capacity and interrupt structure.
outline: 8-bit versus 16-bit data bus; 16 versus 20 address lines
64 KB memory space versus 1 MB, and the segment-plus-offset scheme
8085 is sequential; 8086 has a BIU and a 6-byte queue giving overlap
Flag and register sets compared; segment registers exist only in the 8086
Interrupt handling: 8085 has 5 hardware interrupts and 8 RST vectors, 8086 has a 256-entry vector table
Conclusion: a fair judgement of which suits small control tasks and which suits larger programs

bank.q: Explain why the 8086 multiplexes address and data on AD0–AD15. Show how latches solve the problem and what goes wrong if the latch is removed.
outline: 44-pin package limits the number of pins available
During T1 the lines carry address; ALE marks the valid address time
During T2 and T3 the same lines are used for data
8282 latch clocked by ALE stores the address for the whole bus cycle
Without the latch, memory would see the address change mid-cycle and read or write the wrong location
Also mention A16/S3 to A19/S6 which carry status bits instead of data

bank.q: Compare full address decoding with partial decoding in a microprocessor-based system. State which one you would choose for a small 8085 instrument and why.
outline: Full decoding uses all unused address lines, so every address selects exactly one device
Partial decoding ignores some lines, so the device appears at many mirror addresses
Effect on memory map, on future expansion and on the cost of the decoder gates
I/O map and the IO/M signal decide whether the address is memory or port space
Recommendation with reason: full decoding for a clean map, partial decoding only where the address space is fixed and cheap
Mention the risk of two devices answering the same address if decoding is careless

glossary.def: A single chip containing the CPU, with no built-in memory or I/O peripherals.
The register that holds one operand and receives the result in most arithmetic and logical instructions.
Arithmetic and logic unit; the block that adds, subtracts, ANDs, ORs, rotates and compares.
A single flip-flop that records one property of the last result, such as zero, carry or parity.
The part of an instruction byte that tells the CPU which operation to perform.
The complete sequence of fetching, decoding and executing one instruction.
One clock period of the processor; timing diagrams are drawn in T-states.
A group of T-states that completes one bus operation.
Address latch enable; a pulse in T1 of the 8085 that tells external latches to capture the low address byte.
A bus that carries two different things, such as address and data, on the same pins at different times.
An extra T-state inserted when slow memory pulls READY low, stretching the machine cycle.
The 8086 unit that drives the buses, computes physical addresses and prefetches instructions.
The 8086 unit that decodes and executes the instructions supplied from the queue.
A 6-byte first-in-first-out store of prefetched instruction bytes in the 8086.
One of CS, DS, SS or ES; it holds the starting paragraph of a 64 KB segment.
The 20-bit address placed on the bus, computed as segment × 16 + offset.
8086 configuration in which the processor generates all its own bus control signals.
8086 configuration in which status lines are decoded by the 8288 to produce bus control signals.
An input that enables a memory or I/O chip only when the address belongs to that chip.
A logic block that turns a group of address bits into separate active outputs, one per device.
An instruction such as MOVSB or CMPSB that works on a block of bytes or words through SI and DI.
Direct memory access; a controller such as the 8237 moves data to or from memory without the CPU handling each byte.
The address the CPU jumps to when a particular interrupt is accepted.
